title: Parmenides
orientation: Where Heraclitus said everything changes, Parmenides retorted that nothing changes at all: he argued from the nature of thought and language to the conclusion that the 'One' -- indivisible, unchanging being -- is the only reality, and that the world of sensible, changing things is mere illusion. It matters because Russell treats this as the first example in philosophy of an argument running from language and logic straight to conclusions about the world, a pattern that recurs in most subsequent metaphysics down to and including Hegel, and because Russell uses it to introduce, and to criticize in detail, the philosophical concept of 'substance'.
historical_background: Parmenides was a native of Elea in southern Italy and flourished in the first half of the fifth century B.C. According to Plato, a young Socrates (around 450 B.C.) met and learned from an aged Parmenides, evidence (whether or not the meeting itself is historical) that Plato was influenced by Parmenides' doctrines. South Italian and Sicilian philosophy generally, unlike Ionia's, leaned toward mysticism and religion and was more entangled with Pythagorean mathematics.
philosophical_problems: Is change genuinely possible, or is it, as Parmenides argues, a logical impossibility masking an unchanging underlying reality?
What follows from the fact that thought and language must always be about something -- must words and names always refer to something that exists?
Can something be known or spoken of without existing, in some sense, at the very moment it is known or spoken of?
What is a 'substance', and is it needed to make sense of things persisting through change?

philosophers_discussed.name: Parmenides
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Central subject: argued, in the poem On Nature, that the senses are deceptive, that only 'the One' (an infinite, indivisible, unchanging being) truly exists, and that becoming and change are impossible, since 'what is' cannot come from 'what is not'.

schools_discussed: The Eleatic school (implicitly, via Parmenides' base at Elea)

core_concepts.name: The One (Parmenidean Being)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Parmenides held that behind all the changing things we perceive with our senses, there is really only one single, unchanging, indivisible thing -- 'the One' -- and that our impression of a changing multiplicity of things is an illusion produced by unreliable senses.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The sole true reality in Parmenides' metaphysics: infinite, indivisible, and (though apparently conceived as material and extended, even spherical) not composed of parts or opposites, since Parmenides denies that opposites (e.g. hot/cold, light/dark) are anything more than the presence or absence of a single quality.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Introduces, for the first time in the tradition Russell is tracing, a fully worked-out metaphysics of unchanging Being set logically against Heraclitus's flux, and supplies the ancestor of the philosophical concept of substance that dominates Western metaphysics, psychology, physics, and theology for over two thousand years.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out in Parmenides' poem On Nature, divided into 'the way of truth' and 'the way of opinion'.
examples: Parmenides' description of the One as a kind of sphere, present as a whole everywhere and therefore indivisible
objections: Russell's own objection: the argument rests on the false assumption that words have a wholly constant meaning, ignoring that the same name can correspond to different mental content for different speakers or at different times
competing_positions: Heraclitus's doctrine of universal flux and the many
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly shapes Plato's doctrines (via a reported meeting with Socrates); more generally introduces the idea, retained by 'subsequent philosophy down to quite modern times', of 'the indestructibility of substance' as the persistent subject of varying predicates.

core_concepts.name: The argument from thought and language to the existence of their objects
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Parmenides argued that since you cannot think or speak about nothing, whatever you think or speak about must in some sense exist -- and since you can think or speak of the same thing at different times, it must exist at all those times, which rules out anything ever really coming into being or ceasing to be.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Parmenides' inference that 'the thing that can be thought and that for the sake of which the thought exists is the same', so that thought and language necessarily have objects existing independently of the act of thinking or speaking, and since such objects can be referred to at any time, they must persist unchangingly through all time.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls this 'the first example in philosophy of an argument from thought and language to the world at large', a pattern of reasoning he says recurs throughout the history of metaphysics, and he devotes much of the chapter to showing exactly where and why it fails (the false assumption that words have fixed, constant meanings).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Stated in the surviving fragments of Parmenides' 'way of truth'.
examples: 'Thou canst not know what is not... for it is the same thing that can be thought and that can be.'
Russell's own worked example: what it means to talk about 'George Washington' long after his death, versus talking about a fictional figure like 'Hamlet' or an imagined species like 'unicorns'
objections: Russell's rebuttal: words do not have a wholly fixed meaning across speakers or times (what 'George Washington' means to Washington himself, to his contemporaries, and to us today all differ), so the fact that we can still meaningfully use his name today does not show he still exists
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes this style of argument 'is to be found in most subsequent metaphysicians down to and including Hegel'.

core_concepts.name: Substance as the persistent subject of predicates
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Later philosophers did not accept Parmenides' extreme claim that nothing at all can change, but they kept a softened version of his idea: that behind changing appearances there must be some persisting 'substance' that stays the same while its properties change.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The concept, which Russell says later philosophy 'accepted from Parmenides' in place of the impossibility of all change, of substance as 'the persistent subject of varying predicates' -- a concept that 'became, and remained for more than two thousand years, one of the fundamental concepts of philosophy, psychology, physics, and theology.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Shows how a refuted philosophical claim (total denial of change) can still leave a lasting, more moderate legacy (belief in persisting substance) that shapes the entire subsequent tradition -- an example, for Russell, of how philosophical refutations are rarely final.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Implicit already in Parmenides' immediate successors, even though the word 'substance' itself does not occur in them.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says he will 'have much to say about it at a later stage', flagging substance as a recurring topic throughout the rest of the book.

arguments.title: Parmenides' argument against the possibility of change
premises: You cannot think of, or meaningfully name, what does not exist ('thou canst not know what is not').
Whenever you think of or name something, that something must exist at the time of thinking or naming.
You can think of or name the same thing at different times (e.g. yesterday and today).
arguments.conclusion: Whatever can be thought or named must exist at all times it is thought or named; therefore nothing genuinely comes into being or passes away, and change is impossible.
arguments.explanation: Russell reconstructs the argument as resting on the assumption that words and thoughts must correspond to something existing independent of, and persisting beyond, any particular act of thinking or speaking.
objections: Russell's central objection: the argument silently assumes words have one constant meaning across all speakers and times, which is false -- e.g. what 'George Washington' means differs for Washington himself, his contemporaries, and us; the correct account is that later uses of the name refer via memories, records, and descriptions, not via the direct persistence of the named object.
implications: If sound, would rule out any genuine change or coming-to-be/passing-away in the world.
Its refutation nonetheless leaves behind the more moderate, historically durable idea of a persisting 'substance' underlying change.

arguments.title: Russell's reply: reference through descriptions rather than persistence of the referent
premises: When we use a name like 'George Washington' today, we are not directly perceiving or thinking of the man himself, since we never knew him.
What is actually present to our minds is some description, image, memory, or record associated with the name (e.g. 'the first President of the United States').
In most true sentences, such a descriptive phrase can be substituted for the proper name without changing the sentence's truth or falsehood.
arguments.conclusion: We can meaningfully and truly speak of past or fictional entities without those entities themselves needing to exist now; Parmenides' inference from 'we can still speak of X' to 'X must still exist' is therefore invalid.
arguments.explanation: Russell uses the imagined cases of Hamlet and unicorns to show that statements apparently 'about' non-existent things are really about words, descriptions, and the works (e.g. Shakespeare's plays, bestiaries) that use them, defusing Parmenides' argument without denying that we can meaningfully discuss the past or the fictional.
objections: An imagined reply from Parmenides himself: if memory is a source of knowledge, and memory occurs now, then in some sense the past must 'be before the mind now' and so still exist in some sense -- a challenge Russell explicitly declines to resolve fully, deferring to a later discussion of memory.
implications: Illustrates Russell's general methodological point that philosophical refutations are rarely final and can usually be revived in modified form.
Anticipates themes in the philosophy of language and reference that Russell developed at length elsewhere in his own work (e.g. theory of descriptions).

key_distinctions: The 'way of truth' versus the 'way of opinion' in Parmenides' poem
Being (what is, eternal and unchanging) versus not-being (what is not, unthinkable and unspeakable)
The persistence of an object versus the persistence, and gradual transformation, of the meaning of a name for that object
Endless duration in time versus eternity as existing wholly outside time (Russell attributes the latter conception specifically to Parmenides, not to Heraclitus)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Parmenides directly answers Heraclitus's doctrine of universal flux (Chapter IV) with the opposite extreme; he was influenced, to an uncertain degree, by Pythagoras and the mathematical/mystical culture of Magna Graecia (Chapter III).
connections_to_later_philosophers: Plato is said to have been influenced by Parmenides, reportedly through a direct meeting with Socrates; the concept of substance introduced here as a successor to Parmenides' 'One' becomes, in Russell's account, one of the fundamental and recurring concepts of the rest of the book; Russell also notes this style of language-to-metaphysics argument recurs 'down to and including Hegel'.
religion_science_culture_context: Parmenides is grouped, geographically and temperamentally, with the more mystical and religious south-Italian/Sicilian philosophical culture (as opposed to the scientific, sceptical Ionians), though Russell stresses that what makes him historically important is a specifically logical, not religious, form of argument.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Parmenides as the inventor not of logic itself but of 'metaphysics based on logic' -- the first philosopher to argue directly from the nature of thought and language to sweeping conclusions about reality. He walks through Parmenides' argument in detail, reconstructs it charitably, and then subjects it to sustained criticism, using the examples of George Washington, Hamlet, and unicorns to show that the argument rests on a false assumption that words possess one constant meaning across speakers and times. Even so, Russell credits the argument with lasting philosophical influence, since it seeded the durable (and, in his view, more defensible) later concept of substance as the persisting subject of change. He is careful to note that refutations of important philosophical theories are 'seldom final', and stages an imagined Parmenidean rebuttal about memory that he explicitly leaves unresolved, to be taken up later in the book.
key_takeaways: Parmenides argued, against Heraclitus, that change is logically impossible and that only a single, unchanging 'One' truly exists; sensory experience of a changing, plural world is illusion.
His central argument runs from the nature of thought and language (you cannot think or name what does not exist) to the conclusion that whatever can be named must exist at all times it is named.
Russell rebuts this by showing that words do not have a fixed, constant meaning across speakers and times, using the examples of 'George Washington', 'Hamlet', and 'unicorns'.

Even though Parmenides' extreme conclusion (no change at all) was rejected, later philosophy kept a moderated version of his insight: the concept of 'substance' as a persisting subject of changing predicates, which shaped philosophy, psychology, physics, and theology for over two thousand years.
Russell calls this the first example in philosophy of an argument running from thought/language directly to conclusions about reality, a pattern he traces forward 'down to and including Hegel'.
study_notes:
The most useful way to read this chapter is as a worked example of how Russell does philosophy, not just history of philosophy: he does not simply report that Parmenides was wrong, he reconstructs the argument as carefully and charitably as he can, and then locates precisely where it goes wrong (the hidden assumption of fixed word-meaning). Try to state Parmenides' argument in your own words before reading Russell's diagnosis, and then check whether you can see, independently, why 'George Washington' can be used truly today without Washington himself needing to exist now.

Also notice the chapter's self-aware methodological aside: Russell stages an imagined comeback from Parmenides about memory (if we can know the past through memory, and memory happens now, doesn't the past have to 'be' now too?), and explicitly declines to settle it, promising a fuller discussion of memory later. This is a good moment to appreciate that Russell treats the history of philosophy as unfinished business -- old arguments get revived in new forms, and 'refutations are seldom final... only a prelude to further refinements.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Parmenides' name for the single, unchanging thing he believed is the only real thing in the universe, behind the illusion of many changing things.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The sole reality in Parmenides' metaphysics: infinite and indivisible being, conceived as extended (even sphere-like) yet without genuine internal division or opposition, since Parmenides denies that 'opposites' like hot and cold are anything more than the presence or absence of one quality.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that behind all the changing properties of a thing, there is some underlying 'it' that stays the same and has those properties.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The persistent subject of varying predicates; a concept Russell says later philosophy accepted from Parmenides in a moderated form, replacing his outright denial of change, and which remained central to philosophy, psychology, physics, and theology for over two thousand years.

glossary_terms.term: Way of truth / way of opinion
glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The two parts of Parmenides' poem: one describing what is really, truly the case (the unchanging One), and one describing the deceptive world as it merely appears to the senses.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Parmenides' division of his poem On Nature into 'the way of truth', concerning unchanging Being accessible to reason, and 'the way of opinion', concerning the illusory world of sensory appearance -- of which only the former survives in enough detail to reconstruct.

questions.prompt: What is Parmenides' central conclusion, and how does it directly oppose Heraclitus?
questions.answer: Parmenides concludes that change is impossible and only a single, unchanging, indivisible 'One' truly exists; this directly opposes Heraclitus's doctrine that everything is in perpetual flux.
questions.explanation: Russell opens the chapter by framing Parmenides as the polar opposite response to Heraclitus within the same early Greek debate about change versus permanence.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Parmenides' argument from the nature of thought and language to the impossibility of change.
questions.answer: Premise: you cannot think of or name what does not exist. Premise: therefore, whatever is thought or named must exist at the moment it is thought or named. Premise: the same thing can be thought or named at different times. Conclusion: whatever can be named must exist at all times it is named, so nothing truly comes into being or passes away.
questions.explanation: Russell calls this the first argument in philosophy running from thought and language to a conclusion about reality at large.

questions.prompt: What is Russell's central objection to Parmenides' argument?
questions.answer: That it falsely assumes words have one constant meaning across all speakers and all times; in fact no two people (and no one person at different times) associate exactly the same mental content with a name, so the ability to keep using a name meaningfully does not require its original object to still exist.
questions.explanation: Russell develops this objection using the examples of George Washington, Hamlet, and unicorns.

questions.prompt: Compare how Russell says we can meaningfully talk about George Washington (a real, past person) versus Hamlet (a fictional character).
questions.answer: Talking about George Washington is really talking, via present memories, records, or descriptions ('the first President of the United States'), about someone who really existed in the past. Talking about Hamlet is really talking about what Shakespeare wrote ('Shakespeare says there was a Prince of Denmark called Hamlet'); 'Hamlet' is not really anyone's name, since no one is actually called Hamlet, though it is imagined to be a name.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this contrast to show that in neither case does the named object need to exist now for our statements to be true or meaningful, refuting Parmenides' inference.

questions.prompt: What concept does Russell say later philosophy 'accepted from Parmenides' in place of his outright denial of all change?
questions.answer: The concept of substance -- the persistent subject of varying predicates -- which remained fundamental to philosophy, psychology, physics, and theology for over two thousand years.
questions.explanation: This shows how a rejected extreme claim can still leave a lasting, moderated philosophical legacy.

quiz.explanation: Parmenides was a native of Elea in southern Italy.

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's main objection to Parmenides' argument that whatever can be named must still exist?
options: That names never refer to anything at all
That the argument falsely assumes words keep one constant meaning across speakers and times
That Parmenides never actually wrote this argument down
That only mathematical objects can be named meaningfully
